summary: Specifies how to extend the RPSL inetnum class to point to geofeed CSV files that tell where IP addresses are, with an optional RPKI-based way to authenticate those files. It obsoletes RFC 9092.

plainLanguage.summary: Address owners can publish a list saying roughly where their addresses are, and sign it so others can trust it.

questions: how to find geofeed data for an ip address
what is the geofeed attribute in inetnum
subtitle: How to find the geofeed file for an IP address, and how to check that its owner really published it.

tldr.problem: RFC 8805 defines geofeed files that tie IP addresses to places, but it does not say how to find the right file for a given IP address, or how to trust it.
tldr.mechanism: Registry inetnum: objects carry a single HTTPS URL to a geofeed file, either in a remarks: line or a geofeed: attribute, and the file may optionally carry an RPKI-based signature.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 9092. Consumers use the most specific inetnum: with a geofeed reference, ignore other location hints, and fetch no more often than weekly without a caching signal.

today: RFC 9632 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 9092. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Geofeeds Need a Finder
sections.content:
Services often tailor themselves to where a user is, usually guessing from the source IP address, which may not point to a user. Operators may also want to publish where their infrastructure is. RFC 8805 defines geofeed, a syntax that associates places with IP addresses, but it does not say how to find the right file for a given address.

This document extends the RPSL inetnum: class to point at geofeed files and says how to use them prudently. Wherever inetnum: is mentioned, inet6num: is assumed too.

It obsoletes RFC 9092. Changes include: RIPE has implemented the geofeed: attribute; having both a remarks: and a geofeed: reference is allowed but discouraged; the authentication section is rewritten and stresses it is optional; geofeed files are only UTF-8 CSV; the IP Address Delegation extension must not use inherit; and when geofeed data exist, other location hints should be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Many sites want to know roughly where a visitor is. There is a list format for that, but nobody said where to find the list. This RFC says where.

sections.title: Pointing at Geofeeds from inetnum:
sections.content:
An inetnum: object describes an IP address range, and these objects form a hierarchy over the address space. Until a registry supports a proper attribute, the pointer is a remarks line whose token Geofeed is case sensitive, followed by one HTTPS URL. Where the registry supports it, the pointer is a geofeed: attribute followed by a single URL. Either way it MUST refer to only a single geofeed file.

inetnum: 192.0.2.0/24 # example
geofeed: https://example.com/geofeed

Consumers MUST be able to read both the remarks: and geofeed: forms until all registries have migrated. An inetnum: SHOULD have at most one geofeed reference, and if both kinds are present, the geofeed: attribute MUST be used.

For objects covering the same range, a signed file MUST be preferred over an unsigned one. If none or several are signed, the one with the most recent last-modified: wins. Only an unsigned file MAY be referenced by multiple inetnum: objects or contain prefixes from more than one registry. Geofeed data may be finer-grained than the inetnum: that refers to it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address block has an entry in a public register. The entry gets one extra line saying, here is the web address of my location list.

sections.title: Fetching and Reading Geofeed Data
sections.content:
For large-scale collection, a registry's FTP service SHOULD be used instead of hammering its WHOIS service. RDAP also carries geofeed data but SHOULD NOT be used for bulk retrieval.

For a given address range, the most specific inetnum: object with a geofeed reference MUST be used. In the RFC's example, a lookup for 192.0.2.0/29 must ignore the geofeed of the enclosing 192.0.0.0/22 because the 192.0.2.0/24 object has its own.

When reading an unsigned file, data outside the referring object's address range MUST be ignored. If geofeed data are specified, other geographic hints such as country:, geoloc: and DNS geoloc records MUST be ignored for that range, because those tend to be administrative rather than where services are deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: When two notes could apply to your street, you follow the one for the smaller area, and you ignore any older guesses about where things are.

sections.title: Optional Signing with RPKI
sections.content:
The WebPKI protects the HTTPS fetch but cannot show who was assigned an IP address space. The RPKI can. A single optional authenticator MAY be appended to a geofeed file: a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) detached signature over the canonical file, made with the key of an RPKI certificate that covers the address range.

Canonical form is UTF-8 with CRLF line ends and no trailing blank lines. The signature is DER encoded, Base64 encoded and wrapped to 72 or fewer characters. The signing certificate MUST cover all prefixes in the file, MUST NOT include the AS Identifier extension, and MUST NOT use inherit in its IP Address Delegation extension. The CA SHOULD sign only one file per key, and MUST issue a new one-time-use end entity certificate for each signing.

Validation has six steps: match the SubjectKeyIdentifier, check the certificate is on the current manifest and covers its resources, validate the certification path, verify the CMS signature, confirm the content type OID id-ct-geofeedCSVwithCRLF, and confirm the address ranges are all covered. Every step MUST succeed.

The signature is hidden as comment lines (each starting with a hash sign) at the end of the file, bracketed by lines reading RPKI Signature: and End Signature:, with an address range that MUST match the inetnum: that points to the file. The CMS signature does not cover those lines.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature is like a wax seal on the list. Only the real owner of the addresses has the stamp, and anyone can check the seal against a public record.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
To register a geofeed, an operator coordinates with their RIR, NIR or the LIR that assigned them addresses. Geofeed files MUST be published and fetched using HTTPS. If a file is signed and the signer's certificate changes, the signature MUST be updated.

Aggregating and republishing geofeed data outside the RPSL model should be avoided, since detailed data from one party could wrongly affect another's, and readers could no longer run the checks in Sections 4 and 5.

To avoid load, fetchers MUST NOT do frequent real-time lookups. Without an HTTP caching signal, collectors SHOULD NOT fetch more often than weekly, and it would be polite to avoid magic times such as midnight UTC or the first of the month.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not keep asking for the list every minute. Check back about once a week, and not at the exact moment everyone else does.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Geofeed data may reveal the approximate location of an IP address, and so perhaps of an individual user. RFC 8805 gives no guidance on reducing that exposure, so operators should be aware and cautious when publishing pointers to geofeed files. All privacy considerations of Section 4 of RFC 8805 apply.

Where RFC 8805 provided the ability to publish location data, this document makes bulk access to it readily available. The RFC says this is a goal, not an accident.
sections.plainLanguage: A list of where addresses are can hint at where people are. Publish it carefully, because this RFC makes it easy for everyone to download it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Consumers should cross-check geofeed data against other sources and SHOULD fetch and process the data themselves, since using a third party's processed data places significant trust in it. All security considerations of RFC 8805 apply.

Some registries have weak or no authentication, which allows spoofed inetnum: objects pointing to malicious files. For example, if a /16 inetnum: points to a signed file, an attacker could publish an unsigned /24 inetnum: in a weakly protected registry and exploit the most-specific-wins rule. Mandatory signatures would stop that, but the RFC says that is not happening anytime soon. Geofeed servers will likely also need to throttle heavy queriers, as registries already do.
sections.plainLanguage: Because anyone might be able to add a fake note to a weakly guarded register, signed lists are safer, though signing is not required.

inetnum: 192.0.2.0/24 # example
remarks: Geofeed https://example.com/geofeed

inetnum: 192.0.2.0/24 # example
geofeed: https://example.com/geofeed
